extracted.intended_audience: contributors to mathlib (users and PR authors for the Lean theorem prover library)
extracted.subtask_description: A project-specific style guide describing the conventions and quality criteria for formalizations contributed to mathlib, the Lean theorem prover library. Covers naming, layout, proof/tactic style, API/abstraction boundaries, documentation, performance, and other conventions to make contributions readable, maintainable, and idiomatic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventional single-letter names map to standard meanings to improve readability and predictability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: `u`, `v`, `w` — universes; `α`, `β`, `γ` — generic types; `a`, `b`, `c` — propositions (or arbitrary terms); `x`, `y`, `z` — elements of generic types; `h`, `h₁`, `h₂` — assumptions / hypotheses; `p`, `q`, `r` — predicates and relations; `s`, `t` — lists and sets; `m`, `n`, `k` — natural numbers; `i`, `j`, `k` — integers; Uppercase (`G`, `R`, `K`, `𝕜`, `E`) — types with mathematical content (groups, rings, fields, vector spaces). Use these conventions so readers can infer meaning from names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layout
rubrics_metrics.description: Formatting and whitespace rules for source files to ensure consistent, readable code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Line length ≤ 100 characters. Indent 2 spaces. Put spaces around `:`, `:=`, and infix operators. Place operators at the end of a line, not the start. Multi-line theorem statements are indented 4 spaces; proofs are indented 2. Put `by` at the end of the preceding line (never alone). These rules standardize appearance and make diffs / reviews easier to read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventions for naming theorems, types, classes, and other declarations so users can predict and find names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem names read as English: `A_of_B_of_C` proves `A` from `B` and `C`. Examples: `add_le` for additive ≤, `mul_pos` for product positivity. Use `snake_case` for propositions/proofs, `UpperCamelCase` for types/structures, and `lowerCamelCase` for other terms. Class names that are nouns begin with `Is` (e.g. `IsNormal`); adjectival classes may omit the `Is` prefix. Aim for idiomatic, discoverable names so library users can guess names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer putting arguments before the colon rather than encoding them in an arrow/hypothesis type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer `example (n : ℝ) (h : 1 < n) : 0 < n := ...` rather than `example (n : ℝ) : 1 < n → 0 < n := ...`. This makes dependencies and implicitness clearer and aligns with common mathlib patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactic style
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventions for writing tactic-mode proofs to maximize clarity and robustness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce subgoals with the focusing dot `·` (not indented). Use one tactic per line; short sequences may use `;`. Do not 'squeeze' a terminal `simp` unless for performance reasons—unsqueezed calls survive lemma renames. Avoid `erw` and extra `rfl` as they often signal missing API or lemmas. Use `case` for named subgoals. These rules favor maintainability and clearer tactic scripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: have/show proof style
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred layout for local `have`/`show` declarations depending on proof length and style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short `have`: `have h1 : P := proof` on a single line. Long `have`: put the proof on the next line indented 2 spaces. With tactic proofs: `have h : P := by tac`. The guide prescribes one-line vs multi-line forms to keep proofs compact but readable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calc blocks
rubrics_metrics.description: Formatting for `calc` chains to keep relations aligned and readable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write `calc` blocks like: `calc a = b := h1  _ ≤ c := h2  _ < d := h3`. Align relations across lines; underscores should be left-justified. This alignment clarifies the chained reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymous functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred notation for short anonymous functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use `fun ... ↦` (the `\mapsto` arrow) rather than `λ` or `=>`. For very simple functions, use the dot notation `·`, e.g. `(· ^ 2)`. This encourages concise, idiomatic code that matches library style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a single canonical form when multiple equivalent formulations exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathlib standardizes equivalent statements to one 'normal form'. Examples: in types with bottom, write `x ≠ ⊥` in hypotheses and `⊥ < x` in conclusions; in types with top, write `x ≠ ⊤` in hypotheses and `x < ⊤` in conclusions. Picking normal forms aids searchability and consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventions for declaration reducibility and API boundaries to balance performance and usability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default to `semireducible`. Prefer type synonyms over `irreducible` when creating API boundaries. Use `irreducible_def` only with documented justification. These choices affect reduction behavior, API stability, and performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module docstrings
rubrics_metrics.description: Required top-of-file documentation to orient readers and future maintainers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every file must start with a docstring containing: a title; contents summary; main definitions and theorems; proof techniques used; notation introduced; and literature references. This documentation makes modules discoverable and usable by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance (PR benchmarking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance must be considered for contributions; PRs are benchmarked to prevent regressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All PRs are benchmarked; negative regressions must be explained or fixed. Performance regressions are treated seriously because they affect library compilation time and user experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deprecation policy
rubrics_metrics.description: How to deprecate public names and retain compatibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the `@[deprecated]` attribute on removed public names. Keep aliases around for 6 months after deprecation to give users time to migrate. This preserves API stability and gives downstream code time to update.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readable (quality criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good formalization should be readable by someone other than the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write proofs, names, and documentation so that other contributors can understand and review the work. Use conventions (layout, naming, docstrings) that improve human readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idiomatically named (quality criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Names should follow mathlib idioms so library users can guess them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose names that fit established patterns (e.g. `add_le`, `mul_pos`) and casing conventions; this increases discoverability and lowers the cognitive load for users searching the library.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performant (quality criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalizations should not unduly slow compilation or execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design APIs and proofs with performance in mind; benchmark PRs and avoid constructs that materially regress compilation time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintainable (quality criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributions should be easy to maintain and resilient to future refactors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hacks that break under renames or API changes (e.g. avoid squeezing terminal `simp`); prefer stable, well-documented abstractions and idiomatic tactics to ease future changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent (quality criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow neighboring mathlib conventions so the codebase feels coherent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere to project-wide conventions (variable names, normal forms, naming schemes, layout) so that new files integrate smoothly with existing code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documented (quality criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modules and declarations must be documented so users know what is provided and how to use it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide module docstrings and document main definitions/theorems; include notation and references. Good documentation supports reuse and understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: API-shaped (quality criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalizations should be designed so others can build on the API provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure definitions and lemmas to expose a stable, useful API (use type synonyms rather than `irreducible` where appropriate, mark deprecations, keep aliases temporarily). Consider how downstream users will import and rely on your declarations.
